displayQuote: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence

meta.title: Who really said "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Carl Sagan wrote it in The Dragons of Eden (1977), page 7 — but he did not coin it. The maxim was in print by December 1895, credited to Dugald Bell.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence'?
meta.ogDescription: Sagan really wrote these eight words in 1977 — but NASA had already credited them to Martin Rees, and a geology journal printed them in 1895.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Sagan really did write these eight words — in the Introduction to The Dragons of Eden (Random House, 1977), page 7, arguing that neuroscience’s failure so far to localize every higher brain function proves nothing about what future work will find. What he did not do is coin the line. Quote Investigator finds the identical maxim in print in December 1895 ↗, and NASA’s Project Cyclops report had already run it as a chapter epigraph over the name of the cosmologist Martin Rees.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Dragons of Eden: Speculations on the Evolution of Human Intelligence
Random House, New York — 1977 (Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction, 1978)
December 1895, credited to Dugald Bell in The Glacialists’ Magazine (per Quote Investigator) — not by Sagan

source.excerpt: … because they have been unable to isolate and localize all higher brain functions, no future generation of neuroanatomists will be able to achieve this objective. But absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
trail: 3 January 1887 — six of the eight words, at a London learned society. The Reverend William Wright, arguing that thin Egyptian records did not disprove Hittite settlement in southern Palestine, told the Victoria Institute that “the absence of evidence is not evidence.” The paper was printed in the society’s Journal of the Transactions, volume 21, in 1888 — Quote Investigator’s earliest match ↗.

December 1895 — the exact eight words, in a glacial-geology journal. Writing on Scandinavian boulders in The Glacialists’ Magazine, Thomas Sheppard set the maxim in quotation marks and handed the credit to somebody else, remarking that it had been said by Mr. Dugald Bell. QI calls this the exact match ↗ and notes that earlier instances may still be found.

Project Cyclops — the maxim reaches NASA, over Martin Rees’s name. Chapter 2 of the Project Cyclops design study, written up from the Stanford/NASA Ames 1971 summer faculty program and catalogued as NASA CR-114445, opens with the line credited to Rees, and the chapter then argues from it: “evidence in the sense Rees uses the word in the quotation above” (p. 3) ↗.

1977 — Sagan puts it on page 7, and it becomes his. In the Introduction to The Dragons of Eden he uses it against readers who treat a gap in the brain map as proof the territory is empty. Wikiquote sources the sentence to that page ↗ — and then lists the same eight words again under Misattributed, where the aphorism is credited to Rees.
source.excerptNote: The first clause is a conclusion Sagan rejects; the maxim is his rebuttal to it, not his claim.

source.rightsNote: The passage quoted here is from The Dragons of Eden, published by Random House in 1977 ↗, so Sagan’s text remains in copyright in the United States and is excerpted here for identification and comment. The eight-word maxim itself is far older — it was in print by December 1895 — and that Victorian wording is long out of copyright; what is protected is the surrounding prose.

author.name: Carl Sagan
author.heading: About Carl Sagan
author.metaLine: 1934–1996 · American astronomer, planetary scientist & science communicator, Cornell University
author.bio: Carl Sagan was a Cornell planetary scientist who became the best-known science communicator of his generation through Cosmos, and who spent his last years writing about how to tell sound reasoning from bad. The Dragons of Eden, the 1977 book this line comes from, is his speculative account of how human intelligence evolved; it won the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction in 1978. He was also a habitual quoter of other people — Wikiquote’s Sagan page ↗ lists several lines he passed on rather than invented, and files this one among them.

misattribution.heading: Genuine wording, borrowed maxim
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake quote. Sagan wrote it, and it is sourced to a page number in one of his books. What goes wrong is the credit line: the eight words are shared as Sagan’s coinage, and they are not his — they were a working scientists’ maxim in print before he was born.

items.why: Sagan is routinely presented as the source of the phrase. Quote Investigator ↗ traces six of the eight words to a paper the Reverend William Wright read to the Victoria Institute in London on 3 January 1887 (“the absence of evidence is not evidence”), printed in the society’s Journal of the Transactions in 1888 — and finds the exact eight words in The Glacialists’ Magazine for December 1895. QI’s verdict is that the maxim evolved over time and that Sagan helped popularize it long after it was in circulation.

Wikiquote lists the bare aphorism in its Misattributed section for Sagan and credits it to Rees ↗. The documented Rees credit is real and predates Sagan’s book: chapter 2 of NASA’s Project Cyclops report opens with the line over his name, and the text then reasons from it — “evidence in the sense Rees uses the word in the quotation above” (NASA CR-114445, p. 3) ↗. But Rees was born on 23 June 1942 ↗, so the 1895 printing rules him out as originator too.

Because the line reads like a slogan from Sagan’s skeptical late work, it is usually filed under his 1995 book. He does use it there — Wikiquote places it in chapter 12, “The Fine Art of Baloney Detection” ↗, as the antidote to the appeal to ignorance — but the earliest Sagan instance Quote Investigator documents ↗ is The Dragons of Eden in 1977, and there it is about brains, not UFOs.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest credit is a chain rather than a name: a Victorian scientists’ maxim, credited in December 1895 to Mr. Dugald Bell, carried into the space age as a Martin Rees epigraph in NASA’s Project Cyclops report, and made famous by Carl Sagan, who wrote it on page 7 of The Dragons of Eden in 1977. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ is the best account of the route, and it warns that earlier instances may still surface.

context.heading: What silence proves
lead: The line is a rule about what silence is allowed to prove. Sagan reaches for it in the Introduction to The Dragons of Eden against one specific bad inference: because no one had yet isolated and localized every higher brain function, some readers had concluded that no one ever would — and, by extension, that mind must be something other than anatomy. His answer is that a gap in the map is not a hole in the territory.

That is also why the maxim first reached a wide scientific audience through the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. NASA’s Project Cyclops study opened its chapter on life in the universe with the line, credited to Martin Rees, because the report had to justify an expensive search that had so far found nothing at all. The phrase licenses a search without promising a result — which is exactly why Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ finds it in glacial geology in 1895, in a naturalist’s hunt for orchids in 1947, and in speculation about surviving moa in New Zealand in 1953.
context.detailsSummary: The people who used it before Sagan
detailsBody: Between 1887 and 1977 the maxim circulates in precisely the fields where absence is the daily working problem — archaeology, glaciology, natural history, palaeontology. QI records ↗ a bull-pedigree dispute in London’s Live Stock Journal on 16 October 1891 that turns on “the distinction between absence of evidence and evidence of absence”; the Dublin geologist W. J. Sollas attacking the fallacy in the Quarterly Journal of the Geological Society in August 1895; and The Yorkshire Post applying it to vanished boat burials on 14 August 1939.

The modern chain runs through astronomy. After the Project Cyclops epigraph, the astronomer Richard Berendzen used the maxim at a symposium on life beyond Earth reported in December 1972, and Sagan put it into print in 1977. Sagan used it once more, in The Demon-Haunted World (1995): Wikiquote places it in chapter 12, “The Fine Art of Baloney Detection” ↗, where he offers it as the cure for the appeal to ignorance.
context.pull: “It has been remarked by Mr. Dugald Bell that ‘absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.’” — Thomas Sheppard, The Glacialists’ Magazine, December 1895
